EMPLOYER'S DUTY TO SECURE WORKERS' COMPENSATION INSURANCE — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes California's statutory framework governing an employer's duty to secure workers' compensation insurance coverage, as set out in California Labor Code sections 3700 through 3710.1. It is prepared in connection with Acme, Inc. and Jordan Lee.

This information sheet describes the acceptable ways an employer may secure the payment of workers' compensation, the criminal penalties the Labor Code attaches to an employer's failure to do so, the Director of Industrial Relations' stop-order authority over an employer found out of compliance, and the civil-action rights the Labor Code gives an injured employee against an employer who has failed to secure coverage.

This information sheet does not determine whether Acme, Inc. has in fact secured workers' compensation coverage, does not determine whether any specific workplace injury is compensable, and is not a substitute for the actual text of the statutes it describes.

THE MANDATORY DUTY TO SECURE WORKERS' COMPENSATION COVERAGE
California Labor Code § 3700 requires every employer except the state to secure the payment of workers' compensation in one or more of the ways the statute itself lists. Two of those ways are: (a) by being insured against liability to pay compensation by one or more insurers duly authorized to write compensation insurance in California; or (b) by securing from the Director of Industrial Relations a certificate of consent to self-insure, either as an individual employer or as one employer in a group of employers, issued upon proof satisfactory to the Director of ability to self-insure and to pay any compensation that may become due to the employer's employees. A separate provision of the same section, § 3700(c), sets out a further self-insurance certification pathway specifically for counties, cities, and other public entities. Nothing in the text of § 3700 conditions this duty on the employer's number of employees.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Every employer except the state shall secure the payment of compensation in one or more of the following ways:"
  — Cal. Labor Code § 3700 (California Legislative Information text), Lab. Code § 3700 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=3700.)
  "(a) By being insured against liability to pay compensation by one or more insurers duly authorized to write compensation insurance in this state. (b) By securing from the Director of Industrial Relations a certificate of consent to self-insure either as an individual employer, or as one employer in a group of employers, which may be given upon furnishing proof satisfactory to the Director of Industrial Relations of ability to self-insure and to pay any compensation that may become due to his or her employees."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 3700, subd. (a)-(b) (California Legislative Information text), Lab. Code § 3700, subds. (a)-(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=3700.)
  Known gap: Section 3700 excepts "the state" itself from this particular coverage-securing duty and, in the same sentence, defines "state" for purposes of the section to include the superior courts of California; this document does not research or state what alternative mechanism, if any, covers state employees, since that would require researching statutes outside the sections fetched for this document. Subdivision (c) (the public-entity self-insurance pathway) was read but is only summarized, not quoted, here, since it is not the general private-employer rule this clause centers on. This document did not find the statutory text of § 3700 to name the State Compensation Insurance Fund specifically as one of the listed ways to secure coverage; whatever the popular understanding, the two ways quoted here are the private-insurance and self-insurance-certificate mechanisms the statute's own text sets out, and this document does not assume additional mechanisms the fetched text does not state. This is one state's statute, stating a fact about what California law requires of employers generally — not a claim about whether any specific employer has in fact secured coverage.

CRIMINAL PENALTY FOR FAILING TO SECURE COVERAGE
California Labor Code § 3700.5 makes it a misdemeanor for an employer who knew, or who because of the employer's knowledge or experience should reasonably have been expected to know, of the obligation to secure the payment of workers' compensation, to fail to secure it. A first conviction is punishable by up to one year in county jail, or by a fine of up to double the premium amount that would otherwise have been due to secure coverage during the uninsured period (but not less than $10,000), or by both. A second or subsequent conviction is punishable by up to one year in county jail, a fine of triple that premium amount (but not less than $50,000), or both. The statute also allows the court, in its discretion, to charge a first-time offender the costs of investigation, and requires that a repeat offender be charged those costs — payable only after any owed employee benefits, director reimbursement, and other penalty assessments are paid.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "The failure to secure the payment of compensation as required by this article by one who knew, or because of his or her knowledge or experience should be reasonably expected to have known, of the obligation to secure the payment of compensation, is a misdemeanor punishable by imprisonment in the county jail for up to one year, or by a fine of up to double the amount of premium, as determined by the court, that would otherwise have been due to secure the payment of compensation during the time compensation was not secured, but not less than ten thousand dollars ($10,000), or by both that imprisonment and fine."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 3700.5, subd. (a) (California Legislative Information text), Lab. Code § 3700.5, subd. (a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=3700.5.)
  "A second or subsequent conviction shall be punished by imprisonment in the county jail for a period not to exceed one year, by a fine of triple the amount of premium, or by both that imprisonment and fine, as determined by the court, that would otherwise have been due to secure the payment of compensation during the time payment was not secured, but not less than fifty thousand dollars ($50,000)."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 3700.5, subd. (b) (California Legislative Information text), Lab. Code § 3700.5, subd. (b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=3700.5.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes § 3700.5, subdivisions (a) and (b); subdivision (c) (governing costs of investigation and their payment priority) is summarized but not separately quoted. This is one state's criminal statute, stating a fact about the penalty California law attaches to a knowing failure to secure coverage — not a claim about whether any specific employer's conduct meets the statute's knowledge requirement, which only a court can determine.

THE DIRECTOR'S AUTHORITY TO ISSUE A STOP ORDER
Separately from the criminal penalty in § 3700.5, California Labor Code § 3710.1 authorizes the Director of Industrial Relations, upon finding that an employer has failed to secure the payment of compensation as § 3700 requires, to issue and serve on that employer a stop order prohibiting the use of employee labor until the employer comes into compliance with § 3700; the stop order takes effect immediately upon service. Employees affected by the resulting work stoppage must be paid by the employer for time lost, up to 10 days, while compliance is pending. An employer may protest the stop order by filing a written request for a hearing with the director within 20 days of service; the statute requires the hearing to be held within 5 days of that filing, requires the director to mail a written notice of findings within 24 hours after the hearing concludes, and allows the employer to seek a writ of mandate from the findings in superior court within 45 days after the notice is mailed.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Where an employer has failed to secure the payment of compensation as required by Section 3700, the director shall issue and serve on such employer a stop order prohibiting the use of employee labor by such employer until the employer’s compliance with the provisions of Section 3700."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 3710.1 (California Legislative Information text), Lab. Code § 3710.1 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=3710.1.)
  "Any employee so affected by such work stoppage shall be paid by the employer for such time lost, not exceeding 10 days, pending compliance by the employer. Such employer may protest the stop order by making and filing with the director a written request for a hearing within 20 days after service of such stop order."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 3710.1 (California Legislative Information text), Lab. Code § 3710.1 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=3710.1.)
  Known gap: Section 3710.1 gives this stop-order authority to "the director," i.e., the Director of Industrial Relations — the same official named in § 3700(b) as issuing self-insurance certificates — not to the Labor Commissioner, a separate DIR official whose office administers different Labor Code enforcement functions this document does not address. This clause quotes most, but not all, of § 3710.1's procedural sequence; the exact wording governing the content and mailing of the director's post-hearing findings was read but is only summarized, not quoted, here. This is one state's statute, stating a fact about the director's enforcement authority in general — not a claim that any specific employer has been found out of compliance or is subject to a stop order.

AN INJURED EMPLOYEE'S CIVIL ACTION AGAINST AN UNINSURED EMPLOYER
California Labor Code § 3706 states that if an employer fails to secure the payment of compensation, an injured employee (or the employee's dependents) may bring a civil action at law against that employer for damages, as if the workers' compensation division of the Labor Code did not apply — meaning the ordinary exclusive-remedy bar on suing an employer directly does not apply where the employer has failed to secure coverage. Labor Code § 3707 further allows the employee or dependents to attach the employer's property, at any time on or after the action is filed, in an amount fixed by the court, to secure payment of an eventual judgment. Labor Code § 3708 then shifts the burden of proof in that civil action: it is presumed the injury directly resulted from and grew out of the employer's negligence, and the employer bears the burden of rebutting that presumption; the statute also removes the defenses of contributory negligence, assumption of risk, and the fellow-servant rule for the employer in that action, and states that no contract or regulation may restore any of those defenses to the employer.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "If any employer fails to secure the payment of compensation, any injured employee or his dependents may bring an action at law against such employer for damages, as if this division did not apply."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 3706 (California Legislative Information text), Lab. Code § 3706 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=3706.)
  "The injured employee or his dependents may in such action attach the property of the employer, at any time upon or after the institution of such action, in an amount fixed by the court, to secure the payment of any judgment which is ultimately obtained."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 3707 (California Legislative Information text), Lab. Code § 3707 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=3707.)
  "In such action it is presumed that the injury to the employee was a direct result and grew out of the negligence of the employer, and the burden of proof is upon the employer, to rebut the presumption of negligence."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 3708 (California Legislative Information text), Lab. Code § 3708 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=3708.)
  "It is not a defense to the employer that the employee was guilty of contributory negligence, or assumed the risk of the hazard complained of, or that the injury was caused by the negligence of a fellow servant. No contract or regulation shall restore to the employer any of the foregoing defenses."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 3708 (California Legislative Information text), Lab. Code § 3708 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=3708.)
  Known gap: Sections 3706, 3707, and 3708 are three separate, independently numbered sections of the same statutory chapter (Chapter 4, Compensation Insurance and Security), so while each was independently fetched and verified, they are not independent in the sense of being separately enacted bodies of law — they operate together as one linked remedy scheme. Section 3708's presumption-and-lost-defenses rule contains a further cross-reference: the statute states it does not apply to an employer of an employee as defined in Labor Code § 3351(d), with respect to that employee, but does apply to employers of employees described in § 3715(b), with respect to those employees. Neither § 3351(d) nor § 3715(b) was independently fetched or verified in this session, so this document does not state what categories of employer or employee those cross-referenced provisions describe; a reader would need to separately check those two sections to know whether this exception applies to a particular employment relationship. This is one state's statute, stating a fact about the civil remedy and evidentiary consequences California law attaches to an employer's failure to secure coverage generally — not a claim about whether any specific employer failed to secure coverage or that any specific employee's action would succeed.

CLOSING AND SIGNATURE BLOCK — WORKERS' COMPENSATION INSURANCE COVERAGE DUTY INFORMATION SHEET
I declare that the information above is true and correct to the best of my knowledge.

Executed on September 1, 2026 at Oakland, California.
